17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+2b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -8 & 2 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 \\ 2 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -8 & 2 & 0 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 & 2 \\ 6 & -8 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 & 6\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-4(\frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3})+2{x}_{3}=-2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2+{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2+{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+2b+c=1+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+0=4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186269136 :question/id #uuid "ef71613a-c794-54f5-9a74-68efbe48ffea" :question/math-academy-id "q-137034"} {:db/id 17592186326894 :question/id #uuid "d34cdae0-7b23-59fc-a8bc-f0d99444106f" :question/math-academy-id "q-40921" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "027310f9-ee0d-507a-bc28-d9da862bc3bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186323994} {:answer/id #uuid "13cbf72a-775b-5500-b4ce-fd7dee8abc45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186324150} {:answer/id #uuid "6058f5f8-765c-528f-b9e3-77d370e52e5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186324776} {:answer/id #uuid "df18dbbf-d1af-5d62-9ba8-07e3f6047abf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186325920} {:answer/id #uuid "df1f5f2f-9dda-564b-8601-3ba072795d25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186325921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186323994} :answer-field/id #uuid "58847018-c5c9-5b9a-9650-5b07e75b721b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326372}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of  $3a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & -3 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & -3 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}54 & -18 \\ -18 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}54 & -18 & 12 \\ -18 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}54 & -18 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{2}{9}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{9}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{9} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
3a+\frac{b}{c}=3\cdot \frac{2}{9}+\frac{(\frac{1}{3})}{1}=1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186326895 :question/id #uuid "c3df77ba-fc93-5eb8-9827-0c8cef3d9027" :question/math-academy-id "q-40923"} {:db/id 17592186326896 :question/id #uuid "5b6fc54b-cb36-5749-9df6-d5883bd36fd6" :question/math-academy-id "q-40927"} {:db/id 17592186326897 :question/id #uuid "db567127-1e8b-50cb-a3d2-dc5e2ea462cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-40950" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133801 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9642ac63-6925-5ea3-925d-e697a6222064" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given in Matrix Form with Collinearity"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06c8cf07-1252-5e91-b5c9-12f38c1f946f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186324034} {:answer/id #uuid "91384dd4-5bcc-5860-814c-f96556460493" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186325204} {:answer/id #uuid "93d14029-007f-54bd-9d2a-0c82c9066807" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186325227} {:answer/id #uuid "a9f7e58b-5b63-5e1f-ae19-6232045969c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186325419} {:answer/id #uuid "b3759c15-e036-5c30-848d-c2b42024912f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186325509}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "06c8cf07-1252-5e91-b5c9-12f38c1f946f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186324034} :answer-field/id #uuid "6314ea6d-cf55-58df-9abc-6434d47d5c83" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186326389}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}b \\ c \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,+\,{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $2a-3b-6c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a-3b-6c=2(\frac{1}{2})-3(1)-6(0)=-2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186326913 :question/id #uuid "85d7c223-d931-53ec-98fb-80a06e5b2764" :question/math-academy-id "q-41904" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133801 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9642ac63-6925-5ea3-925d-e697a6222064" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given in Matrix Form with Collinearity"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3c20af83-4b36-5128-89ee-a2b0f277470a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186324458} {:answer/id #uuid "58d3b34f-653e-5908-8110-49345a2e51c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186324708} {:answer/id #uuid "5c3eb528-5cf9-526f-857f-315ec81f0eb3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186324735} {:answer/id #uuid "b0bbe617-b13b-516f-806c-a9356a26279f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186325479} {:answer/id #uuid "c5751e84-51f5-5505-bf51-a2e74963787c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186325674}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "b0bbe617-b13b-516f-806c-a9356a26279f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186325479} :answer-field/id #uuid "ac5ff18b-ee0a-5c8e-a1ac-a863dbac8c0a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186326532}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $15a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -4 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -4 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}40 & -20 \\ -20 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -5 & 1 \\ -10 & 5 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}10 & -5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
15a+\frac{b}{c}=15\cdot \frac{1}{10}+\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{1}=2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367436 :question/id #uuid "8e0db89b-f0c6-50f0-a4df-0e579944e4eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-137033" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c464ae52-c792-5966-9d49-a2e4829b9b98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186367438} {:answer/id #uuid "60181620-1848-5691-9b01-0836bdae2569" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186367439} {:answer/id #uuid "1ffce98a-3785-54ef-a67a-a79256e5e528" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186367440} {:answer/id #uuid "61d68627-501b-5d8d-a22c-84fdf7f0c3a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186367441} {:answer/id #uuid "5a336a5d-1d0b-5110-8865-6d48c421f50f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186367442}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367440} :answer-field/id #uuid "ac10a081-d7a4-5b23-9a50-e6500fcd48c6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367437}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]\,+\,{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a-4b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 6 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 6 & -4 & 12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second row, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-(-\frac{3}{2})+2{x}_{3}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1-2{x}_{3} \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a-4b+c=-2-4\cdot (-\frac{3}{2})+0=4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186368554 :question/id #uuid "8912c2e3-5605-5590-8ee8-b25e93901622" :question/math-academy-id "q-42245" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1299ade0-03c4-5049-abac-d1b905ea647d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7" :db/id 17592186368556} {:answer/id #uuid "de3e0276-368e-58fc-81ca-2ba8066692a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186368557} {:answer/id #uuid "ce89137e-5a01-54bb-9780-320b4e37ec64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186368558} {:answer/id #uuid "ce900d5f-43f0-5f77-adbc-98050b478ea1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186368559} {:answer/id #uuid "ba8250d4-f373-5760-9fc7-2ed30b0938ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186368560}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186368557} :answer-field/id #uuid "1812231c-b731-57f0-8e96-cc3da0e4fe33" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186368555}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

what is the value of $a+b+4c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 \\ 4 & -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 & -1 \\ 4 & -4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.

 From the second row, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=-3.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-(-3)+2{x}_{3}=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-4-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4-2{x}_{3} \\ -3 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].

$$

A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ a \\ b\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}c \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R

what is the value of $a+3b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & -4 & 2 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 & 4 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{3}=-2,
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+(-2)=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+3b+c=0+3\cdot (-2)+1=-5.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186415143 :question/id #uuid "d4a26f8e-8621-57f0-b0fb-289f901931d0" :question/math-academy-id "q-136954" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0bd7515d-bc8c-5fbf-b8b7-be4ee29a026e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186415110} {:answer/id #uuid "229bfab5-ba1b-52fe-b0f1-2051f81b3eae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186415111} {:answer/id #uuid "383d6df1-6a22-5c04-94da-26eb4b0bd68d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186415120} {:answer/id #uuid "59b52a2f-1933-53c4-9f7d-6b819b9dbb83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186415122} {:answer/id #uuid "7818ba2a-afff-5ecd-8ff6-f5c7aa948efc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186415124}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415124} :answer-field/id #uuid "54a4eb9e-e422-55cf-a2cc-fe7a41adc569" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415134}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

$$

$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -3 \\ -18 & 54 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

 Hence, the general solution is

:answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268722}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=1 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=4 \\ -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $4a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -14 \\ -14 & 14\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -14 & 7 \\ -14 & 14 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -14 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
4a+\frac{b}{c}=4\cdot (\frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{1}=3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186269139 :question/id #uuid "7264a872-6f66-52f9-bc5f-7b2565f54aa2" :question/math-academy-id "q-137096" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133802 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8bc1e31e-5794-5ae3-8620-6bcaadde6a15" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System With Collinearity"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7360267e-e517-562f-a7ab-234dea8e16b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186267158} {:answer/id #uuid "8a852bda-8769-55af-b974-271e085d782f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186267380} {:answer/id #uuid "abc3d198-0e91-5133-9e31-d766dcdd7bac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186267694} {:answer/id #uuid "df227e4e-6f3a-5099-aa04-1ab50365aa3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186268116} {:answer/id #uuid "f0784891-ea63-5109-abfd-c29f5a65f3e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186268282}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "7360267e-e517-562f-a7ab-234dea8e16b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186267158} :answer-field/id #uuid "5fef7bda-8cd4-5d78-b705-1883723f2fd4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186268579}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=3 \\ -2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=6 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$

what is the value of $a-\frac{3b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & 18 \\ 18 & 36\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -18\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 18 & 36 & -18\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-1-2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a-\frac{3b}{c}=-1-\frac{3(-2)}{1}=5.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186269140 :question/id #uuid "93179ecb-11e4-5253-ab06-7702070386da" :question/math-academy-id "q-137097"} {:db/id 17592186269141 :question/id #uuid "58ba77df-63a2-5a9b-ba59-e2f2dbd16055" :question/math-academy-id "q-137119"} {:db/id 17592186367443 :question/id #uuid "b9b18fd2-40c6-532b-a289-0305c371077f" :question/math-academy-id "q-137090" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133802 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8bc1e31e-5794-5ae3-8620-6bcaadde6a15" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System With Collinearity"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "faba9b8c-2db9-5102-aa65-00748558a463" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186367445} {:answer/id #uuid "e2d0ce5d-e84e-57e4-8a47-bf9cb06a4a06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186367446} {:answer/id #uuid "ec1f8972-dbc3-5adb-b2ee-427452d50a48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186367447} {:answer/id #uuid "8e3fff1f-5172-5721-9989-85b34c09b139" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186367448} {:answer/id #uuid "fb047e4f-69c3-5551-ba4d-0963ccacfe94" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186367449}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ec1f8972-dbc3-5adb-b2ee-427452d50a48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186367447} :answer-field/id #uuid "778fca66-9171-578b-a82f-9dd5127d9503" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186367444}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
{\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=3 \\ 6{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=1 \\ 3{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $-4a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}54 & -18 \\ -18 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}54 & -18 & -9 \\ -18 & 6 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}54 & -18 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{9}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-4a+\frac{b}{c}=-4\cdot (-\frac{1}{6})+\frac{(\frac{1}{3})}{1}=1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367450 :question/id #uuid "f080e633-9838-5e96-8287-b7abe35cec6e" :question/math-academy-id "q-137091"} {:db/id 17592186415139 :question/id #uuid "01d4a87d-4b65-5a4c-9736-928bedaa6703" :question/math-academy-id "q-137086" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0aa14c10-e738-56f6-ba1c-e071a121f17f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "13" :db/id 17592186415109} {:answer/id #uuid "3394fe0c-1ef5-5d2a-acd6-6a75d0644ea8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-10" :db/id 17592186415118} {:answer/id #uuid "796589ac-95c1-56f9-b1db-31d0e03ed1d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186415125} {:answer/id #uuid "a0ae1013-f366-5e65-90ff-b5b5ec91675a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-17" :db/id 17592186415128} {:answer/id #uuid "f6952c2b-bc0a-5679-9e51-c3da4a58655d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-19" :db/id 17592186415132}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415128} :answer-field/id #uuid "ed476833-2f74-5fd6-89de-22e15124bc5f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415138}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $12a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -18 \\ -18 & 54\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 30\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -10 \\ -18 & 54 & 30\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{5}{3}+3{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{3}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
12a+\frac{b}{c}=12\cdot (-\frac{5}{3})+\frac{3}{1}=-17.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186415141 :question/id #uuid "4a92698e-17e4-57b8-8191-7aa9adc0e63f" :question/math-academy-id "q-137092" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29e85101-f9b2-5d74-83c6-aabdd8fc2745" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186415114} {:answer/id #uuid "2baff1db-5ead-50b2-af5a-abe277ae4820" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186415115} {:answer/id #uuid "2ccd28ea-578f-5414-8332-a6408e6df178" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186415116} {:answer/id #uuid "2e8878bb-5944-584d-9b48-2add56ecc5fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186415117} {:answer/id #uuid "8cd78f8e-e662-5c98-aa4d-0c408cd252ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186415126}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415126} :answer-field/id #uuid "a27c023d-32d0-5cf3-ade4-1f1674089f41" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415135}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=1 \\ 4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $6a+\frac{4b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}24 & -12 \\ -12 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}24 & -12 & 4 \\ -12 & 6 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}24 & -12 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
6a+\frac{4b}{c}=6\cdot \frac{1}{6}+\frac{4\cdot \frac{1}{2}}{1}=3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186415142 :question/id #uuid "abb758c7-4ff1-5d36-aa75-96f61271e2e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-137094" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26168406-f1b0-5099-9e07-25cd625153b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186415112} {:answer/id #uuid "28a4b0d8-24a1-5c50-8d0d-3d18a2ad1c94" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186415113} {:answer/id #uuid "37a33051-e1b1-5298-99ef-d2c6766952fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186415119} {:answer/id #uuid "571ff69e-5db2-5300-b1f0-1d3e4bea31c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186415121} {:answer/id #uuid "d61a5d2e-e72e-5b6e-9e93-29e9d0122c9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186415131}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415131} :answer-field/id #uuid "ac3cd328-26f2-53b0-bd30-ec73823e7080" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415136}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

$$

what is the value of $14a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -28 \\ -28 & 56\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -18\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & 9 \\ -28 & 56 & -18\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{9}{14}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{14}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{14} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
14a+\frac{b}{c}=14\cdot \frac{9}{14}+\frac{2}{1}=11.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186133822 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133634 :question/id #uuid "8a39f109-9436-55f8-bbb8-87253668378d" :question/math-academy-id "e-5963"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fda08f5d-4513-5be0-b8c4-475e82f9bf5a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048284}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134372 :question/id #uuid "80e97aa1-dac8-53af-afe4-09e324e932eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-41909"} {:db/id 17592186134373 :question/id #uuid "0680aa30-4775-5c1b-82c5-b722226f12db" :question/math-academy-id "q-41912"} {:db/id 17592186269133 :question/id #uuid "d00d21df-b149-5102-8948-a439a72941dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-136811"} {:db/id 17592186269134 :question/id #uuid "69f4362f-6b4d-5c30-8b5c-dedd940a5e83" :question/math-academy-id "q-136822"} {:db/id 17592186269135 :question/id #uuid "a9599aec-b36e-5461-9425-547d03dffdb7" :question/math-academy-id "q-136875"} {:db/id 17592186367429 :question/id #uuid "9fcaaa14-b976-59cf-b555-9129a6aa2fb9" :question/math-academy-id "q-136821"} {:db/id 17592186424018 :question/id #uuid "130f7ccc-d087-5052-915e-6df794e733bd" :question/math-academy-id "q-136921"} {:db/id 17592186424019 :question/id #uuid "4cb13173-852b-58a2-8c1f-3d6511a05fac" :question/math-academy-id "q-136920"} {:db/id 17592186442296 :question/id #uuid "9375f3f0-3aa6-5a84-b715-8086fa3c68db" :question/math-academy-id "q-136883"} {:db/id 17592186483345 :question/id #uuid "0200c257-e4df-57c1-8eaf-e14f946ede8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-41913"}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing the Normal Equation Corresponding to a Linear System"} {:db/id 17592186133634 :question/id #uuid "8a39f109-9436-55f8-bbb8-87253668378d" :question/math-academy-id "e-5963"} {:db/id 17592186048284 :topic/difficulty 0.7128825119996229 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428682 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. $$

Consider the system of linear equations and its corresponding normal equation shown above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5 & -10 & 5 \\ -10 & 20 & -10 \\ 5 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=20+(-10)+(-6)=4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186483345 :question/id #uuid "0200c257-e4df-57c1-8eaf-e14f946ede8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-41913"} {:db/id 17592186049282} {:db/id 17592186049503} {:db/id 17592186049845} 2167} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134698 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135060 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following inconsistent system of equations:

![](images/6b/6bcdc34077d88eac5ed89d408a1d2525b617a4f427b13433757df918585d380f.svg)

Since the system is inconsistent, we cannot find an exact solution. However, as we've previously seen, we can attempt to find the so-called least-squares solution, which is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\|  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \|
$$

is as small as possible. 

As before, the least-squares solution can be found by solving the corresponding normal equation, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note the following: 

- Previously, we solved the normal equation by left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T A)^{-1}.$

- However, in this case, the second column of $A$ is a multiple of the first.

- So, the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent.

- Therefore, $A^T A$ is not invertible.

To solve the normal equation in this case, we proceed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5 & -20 \\ -20 & 80\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 20\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the last equation by Gaussian elimination, we obtain the general solution

![](images/b9/b93bd5cb988f208eb26115bfaa08e81be989ee79cf3655612c1a0522a5566d95.svg)

Notice that our solution is not unique! The second term of the least-squares solution (highlighted in blue) represents vectors from the null space of $A.$ 

In general, if a matrix $A$ has collinear columns, then the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ is not unique." :tutorial/id #uuid "2f2e227a-264e-5e00-8c12-ea534f4b351f" 17592186415138}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "01d4a87d-4b65-5a4c-9736-928bedaa6703" :question/math-academy-id "q-137086" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=3 \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=1 \\ {x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=-5\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $12a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -18 \\ -18 & 54\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 30\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -10 \\ -18 & 54 & 30\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{5}{3}+3{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{3}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
12a+\frac{b}{c}=12\cdot (-\frac{5}{3})+\frac{3}{1}=-17.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "40c07ba2-e36f-5f6c-9e19-b8d5be6314d0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415145}} {:db/id 17592186415145 :step/content {:db/id 17592186415141 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29e85101-f9b2-5d74-83c6-aabdd8fc2745" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186415114} {:answer/id #uuid "2baff1db-5ead-50b2-af5a-abe277ae4820" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186415115} {:answer/id #uuid "2ccd28ea-578f-5414-8332-a6408e6df178" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186415116} {:answer/id #uuid "2e8878bb-5944-584d-9b48-2add56ecc5fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186415117} {:answer/id #uuid "8cd78f8e-e662-5c98-aa4d-0c408cd252ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186415126}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415126} :answer-field/id #uuid "a27c023d-32d0-5cf3-ade4-1f1674089f41" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415135}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4a92698e-17e4-57b8-8191-7aa9adc0e63f" :question/math-academy-id "q-137092" :question/problem "$$

#uuid "4a92698e-17e4-57b8-8191-7aa9adc0e63f" :question/math-academy-id "q-137092" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=1 \\ 4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $6a+\frac{4b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}24 & -12 \\ -12 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}24 & -12 & 4 \\ -12 & 6 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}24 & -12 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
6a+\frac{4b}{c}=6\cdot \frac{1}{6}+\frac{4\cdot \frac{1}{2}}{1}=3.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b7f52acc-285e-5a90-8147-1ce492061ed5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415148}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29e85101-f9b2-5d74-83c6-aabdd8fc2745" :answer/type {:db/id $$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -14 \\ -14 & 14\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -14 & 7 \\ -14 & 14 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -14 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$

$$

$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

what is the value of $4a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -14 \\ -14 & 14\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -14 & 7 \\ -14 & 14 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -14 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
4a+\frac{b}{c}=4\cdot (\frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{1}=3.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "dc1e81e2-a33c-5ae5-b25d-0e3fcbe639b8"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "71872f14-7cc4-5fb9-8cf7-9ffe96aefe19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -3 \\ -18 & 54 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -28 \\ -28 & 56\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -18\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & 9 \\ -28 & 56 & -18\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{9}{14}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{14}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{14} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
14a+\frac{b}{c}=14\cdot \frac{9}{14}+\frac{2}{1}=11.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7a71b792-bbea-515e-8ba1-f0cd6295bfe8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186491275}} {:db/id 17592186491266 :step/content {:db/id 17592186368554 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1299ade0-03c4-5049-abac-d1b905ea647d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7" :db/id 17592186368556} {:answer/id #uuid "de3e0276-368e-58fc-81ca-2ba8066692a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186368557} {:answer/id #uuid "ce89137e-5a01-54bb-9780-320b4e37ec64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186368558} {:answer/id #uuid "ce900d5f-43f0-5f77-adbc-98050b478ea1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186368559} {:answer/id #uuid "ba8250d4-f373-5760-9fc7-2ed30b0938ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186368560}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186368557} :answer-field/id #uuid "1812231c-b731-57f0-8e96-cc3da0e4fe33" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186368555}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8912c2e3-5605-5590-8ee8-b25e93901622" :question/math-academy-id "q-42245" :question/problem "$$

$$

what is the value of $a+b+4c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 \\ 4 & -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 & -1 \\ 4 & -4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.

 From the second row, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=-3.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-(-3)+2{x}_{3}=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-4-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4-2{x}_{3} \\ -3 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+4c=(-2)+(-3)+4\cdot 0=-5.

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -28 \\ -28 & 56\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -18\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & 9 \\ -28 & 56 & -18\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{9}{14}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{14}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{14} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
14a+\frac{b}{c}=14\cdot \frac{9}{14}+\frac{2}{1}=11.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7a71b792-bbea-515e-8ba1-f0cd6295bfe8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186491275}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "027310f9-ee0d-507a-bc28-d9da862bc3bf" :answer/type {:db/id #uuid "8912c2e3-5605-5590-8ee8-b25e93901622" :question/math-academy-id "q-42245" :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+b+4c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 \\ 4 & -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 & -1 \\ 4 & -4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.

 From the second row, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=-3.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-(-3)+2{x}_{3}=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-4-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4-2{x}_{3} \\ -3 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+4c=(-2)+(-3)+4\cdot 0=-5.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c604cb99-8f2f-571b-8dc3-8a3b1b413bdf" :step/next {:db/id 17592186491220}} {:db/id 17592186491275 :step/content {:db/id 17592186269139 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7360267e-e517-562f-a7ab-234dea8e16b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186267158} {:answer/id #uuid "8a852bda-8769-55af-b974-271e085d782f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186267380} {:answer/id #uuid "abc3d198-0e91-5133-9e31-d766dcdd7bac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186267694} {:answer/id #uuid "df227e4e-6f3a-5099-aa04-1ab50365aa3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186268116} {:answer/id #uuid "f0784891-ea63-5109-abfd-c29f5a65f3e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186268282}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186267158} :answer-field/id #uuid "5fef7bda-8cd4-5d78-b705-1883723f2fd4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268579}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7264a872-6f66-52f9-bc5f-7b2565f54aa2" :question/math-academy-id "q-137096" :question/problem "$$

what is the value of $a-\frac{3b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$

$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & 18 \\ 18 & 36\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -18\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 18 & 36 & -18\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-1-2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a-\frac{3b}{c}=-1-\frac{3(-2)}{1}=5.

"Consider $\triangle ABC$ shown below. 

![](images/6f/6fdb9a8337d16f1ef1910989b3df92844c5393c33108f98ae7993cc939bed0b3.png)

Now, let's draw a line segment that 

- runs from $\color{blue}C$ to the line ${\color{red}\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB}},$ and

- is *perpendicular* to ${\color{red}\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB}}.$

This line segment is the dashed segment shown below:

![](images/4a/4a7ee2771c9b0c60dbb07c43b0439e822ea9b2c261ac41af9b44fec72b9f2a91.png)

Finally, let's label the other endpoint of our segment ${\color{blue}{H}}.$

![](images/75/758eab533719220515460b6677054438a9ac0e2701d1a5267b973e526f63bd90.png)

Note the following:

- The line segment ${\color{blue}\overline{CH}}$ is called the **height** (or **altitude**) *corresponding to* ${\color{red}\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB}}.$

- The line $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB}$ is called the **base** of the altitude ${\color{blue}\overline{CH}}.$

As we'll soon discover, the heights and their corresponding bases are important attributes of triangles." :tutorial/id #uuid "bdb9bfbd-b830-51f0-8712-5d34f83f2812" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2232 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4231f520-72fe-5c14-8733-25cc76a6e65e" :step/math-academy-id 9151 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116397}} {:db/id 17592186116397 :step/content {:db/id 17592186115409 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186114985 :question/id #uuid "972fe403-9a15-5d10-8f9f-f5c93eb586ff" :question/math-academy-id "e-2725"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f7e817a0-edcf-54ca-ba4c-ffe91af04675" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050357}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115646} {:db/id 17592186115952} {:db/id 17592186253495} {:db/id 17592186253496} {:db/id 17592186294864} {:db/id 17592186386882} {:db/id 17592186393737}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Height of a Triangle"} :step/id #uuid "52e4c58c-e58e-5223-98e5-cc31383de47c" :step/math-academy-id 9154 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116398}} {:db/id 17592186116398 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116450 :tutorial/content "We can draw exactly three heights (or altitudes) in any triangle. To demonstrate, consider $\triangle{ABC}$ below.

![](images/df/df1ac2c1074305f8ead506d9aeb8c3927ad51ae5949b45976f1971b52d402ee5.png)

The height corresponding to $\overline{BC}$ is a line segment that 

- runs from the opposite vertex $A$ to the line $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{BC},$ and

- is perpendicular to $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{BC}.$

In this case, it's impossible to draw a perpendicular from $A$ to the *segment* $\overline{BC}.$ However, we can first *extend* the line segment $\overline{BC}$ as follows:

![](images/26/26bf9eb8af1e9b71c263c08cae5797d5c911410985cdc01213ac2c295f7b8d46.png)

Now, we draw the perpendicular from $A$ to $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{BC}.$ This gives the height $\overline{AH}{:}$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]?
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-2I)^{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Given a matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda ,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $k$ is a vector $v$ that satisfies

$$
(A-\lambda I)^{k}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-\lambda I)^{k-1}v\ne 0.
$$

To find a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to $\lambda =2,$ we need to find a vector $v$ that satisfies

$$
(A-2I)^{2}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-2I)v\ne 0.
$$

Let's consider each condition:

- We start by solving $(A-2I)^{2}v=0.$ We're given that

$$
(A-2I)^{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,.
$$

This means that *any* vector in ${R}^{3}$ is a solution to $(A-2I)^{2}v=0.$ Therefore, the solution to $(A-2I)^{2}v=0$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}v=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} \\ {v}_{3}\end{aligned}]={v}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{v}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{v}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we solve $(A-2I)v=0.$ We have

$$
A-2I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,.
$$

This matrix is already in reduced row echelon form. This means that the solution to $(A-2I)v=0$ is ${v}_{2}=0,$ where ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}$ are free variables. Therefore, the solution to $(A-2I)v=0$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}v=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} \\ {v}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} \\ 0 \\ {v}_{3}\end{aligned}]={v}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{v}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the solutions, we see that the vector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ satisfies $(A-2I)^{2}v=0$ but does *not* satisfy $(A-2I)v=0.$ 

Hence, $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ of $A.$"} {:db/id 17592186176572 :question/id #uuid "f57b47a7-70bf-58da-a154-3f2affbc7ee1" $$

$$

To find a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to $\lambda =1,$ we need to find a vector $v$ that satisfies

$$
(A-I)^{2}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-I)v\ne 0.
$$

Let's consider each condition:

- We start by solving $(A-I)^{2}v=0.$ We're given that

$$
(A-I)^{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,.
$$

This means that *any* vector in ${R}^{3}$ is a solution to $(A-I)^{2}v=0.$ Therefore, the solution to $(A-I)^{2}v=0$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}v=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} \\ {v}_{3}\end{aligned}]={v}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{v}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{v}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we solve $(A-I)v=0.$ We have

$$
A-I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,.
$$

This matrix is already in reduced row echelon form. This means that the solution to $(A-I)v=0$ is ${v}_{3}=0,$ where ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are free variables. Therefore, the solution to $(A-I)v=0$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}v=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} \\ {v}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]={v}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{v}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the solutions, we see that the vector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ satisfies $(A-I)^{2}v=0$ but does *not* satisfy $(A-I)v=0.$
