"cb434a73-533d-5a74-927b-b8b1bf69153e" :step/math-academy-id 36389} {:db/id 17592186176824 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177045 :tutorial/content "Let's return to the example of a car traveling at ${\color{red}{40}}$ miles per hour. 

If the car travels at this speed, it covers  a distance of ${\color{red}{40}}$ miles *every hour*. Therefore, we can deduce the following:

- after ${\color{blue}{1}}$ hour, the car covers a distance of ${\color{red}{40}}\times{\color{blue}{1}} = 40$ miles

- after ${\color{blue}{2}}$ hours, the car covers a distance of ${\color{red}{40}}\times{\color{blue}{2}} = 80$ miles

- after ${\color{blue}{3}}$ hours, the car covers a distance of ${\color{red}{40}}\times{\color{blue}{3}} = 120$ miles

- after ${\color{blue}{4}}$ hours, the car covers a distance of ${\color{red}{40}}\times{\color{blue}{4}} = 160$ miles

- $\cdots$

This suggests the following formula:

$$
\text{distance} = \text{speed} \times \text{time}
$$

We can use this formula to calculate the distance traveled by an object moving at a constant speed.

For instance, suppose an elevator traveled for $1.5$ minutes at a constant speed of $120$ feet per minute. What distance is covered by the elevator?

The speed is $120$ feet per minute. To find the distance covered in $1.5$ minutes, we multiply the speed by $1.5.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{distance} & =\text{speed}\times \text{time} \\  & =120\times 1.5 \\  & =180.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the elevator covered a distance of $180$ feet." :tutorial/id #uuid "95f37ad7-7647-57e9-ae85-7a3dcab40f25" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5960 :tutorial/title "Calculating the Distance Traveled by an Object"} :step/id #uuid "02f9ad99-d474-59a2-b870-d4cc8af16598" :step/math-academy-id 36390 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176822}} {:db/id 17592186176825 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177046 :tutorial/content "Let's recall the formula relating distance to speed and time:

$$
\text{speed} \times \text{time} = \text{distance}
$$

Using the relationship between multiplication and division, we can write this equation as

$$
\text{time} = \text{distance} \div \text{speed}
$$

which is equivalent to the formula

$$
\text{time} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}.
$$

We can use this formula to calculate the time taken for an object moving at a particular speed to cover a certain distance. 

For example, suppose a plane flew for $3\,120$ kilometers at a constant speed of $520$ kilometers per hour. For how long was the plane in motion?

To determine the time the plane was in motion, we divide the distance, $3\,120$ kilometers, by the speed, $520$ kilometers per hour. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{time} & =\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}} \\  & =\frac{3\,120}{520} \\  & =\frac{3\,120÷10}{520÷10} \\  & =\frac{312}{52} \\  & =312÷52 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the plane was in motion for $6$ hours." :tutorial/id #uuid "76064dfb-b2e4-56a5-95f7-2a97b1fb392b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5961 :tutorial/title "Calculating the Total Time an Object is in Motion"} :step/id #uuid "1aec8595-c434-5eab-92bb-a1d9a3d99a15" :step/math-academy-id 36391 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176823}}] :activity/title "Speed as a Unit Rate" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176136} {:db/id 17592186176820 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177044 :tutorial/content "**Speed** is a special unit rate applied to moving objects. [{:db/id 17592186074827 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074969 :tutorial/content "We can illustrate ratios with a **tape diagram**, where each box represents a unit.

The tape diagram below shows the ratio between the number of black hair ties and white hair ties there are in the package Anabelle bought.

![](images/15/15c9b0b47bd0e6fdca99ab67df4bdc7e9202978128770df717bb347e463cfb33.png)

In this diagram, each box represents a hair tie.
So, what is the ratio of white hair ties to black hair ties?

The tape diagram for white hair ties shows $\color{blue}5$ boxes, so Anabelle has $\color{blue}5$ white hair ties.

Likewise, the tape diagram for black hair ties contains $\color{red}6$ boxes, so she has $\color{red}6$ black hair ties.

Therefore, the ratio of white hair ties to black hair ties is ${\color{blue}5}:{\color{red}6}$." :tutorial/id #uuid "db49cfe6-f1ac-5798-847e-e351e2ca2271" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2054 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6d46a89c-a25b-5481-b05c-1dc6047fbb36" :step/math-academy-id 633368 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074828}} {:db/id 17592186074828 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073852 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073567 :question/id #uuid "032ead48-0a3f-5a5e-b604-2a2fc0d91770" :question/math-academy-id "e-2288"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bbf7f692-6019-55eb-9fc9-c4cad3c4df93" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050924}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074472} {:db/id 17592186074483}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Ratios From Tape Diagrams"} :step/id #uuid "834b2a5e-aa96-59d4-9f65-37f0c2e561a3" :step/math-academy-id 633369 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074829}} {:db/id 17592186074829 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073853 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073569 :question/id #uuid "fe68a823-4477-5d82-bd17-12842d6e8735" :question/math-academy-id "e-2290"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5ef376fd-9191-586d-b172-5e46e3043243" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074471} {:db/id 17592186074477}] :knowledge-point/title "Creating Tape Diagrams Given a Ratio"} :step/id #uuid "87245d97-a832-5bd2-bb54-0d9029ed3603" :step/math-academy-id 633372 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074830}} {:db/id 17592186074830 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074971 :tutorial/content "In some tape diagrams, each box can represent more than one unit.

For instance, the ratio of pins to paper clips in a case is given by the tape diagram below. If there are $15$ pins in the case, how many paper clips are there in total?

![](images/82/82f94d7377ea3923ffdd825de324b128cd8b4f102070bf6890dee2cbc619657e.png)

We are told that there are $15$ pins in the case, but the tape diagram for pins shows $3$ boxes. Therefore, each box in the diagram above represents

$$
15 \div 3 = 5
$$

units.

Now, we fill the number $5$ in each box of both tapes:

![](images/7d/7d8d1e22ee067588593b7b08442dd2a44142f9f684d84809056ee0ffb4b2dfc0.png)

Since there are $4$ boxes corresponding to paper clips, and each box represents $5$ units, the total number of paper clips is

$$
4 \times 5 = 20 \,
$$

So, there are $20$ paper clips in Mrs. Robinson's case." :tutorial/id #uuid "6a5fc255-be3d-58ad-b9c5-c1bbed5b72ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2056 :tutorial/title "Computing Ratios Using Tape Diagrams With Multiple Units"} :step/id #uuid "e1906855-8771-5209-9808-b6c5d3d82903" :step/math-academy-id 633375 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074831}} {:db/id 17592186074831 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073854 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073574 :question/id #uuid "c089129a-f06b-53d3-a7be-d8d8a79b6dd9" :question/math-academy-id "e-2295"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5aedad19-4881-5b53-9ec9-335bbe9cec48" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074470} {:db/id 17592186074478}] :knowledge-point/title "Interpreting Tape Diagrams Using Multiple Units"} :step/id #uuid "b40ecc8b-3307-5e8c-a52b-105ba265f265" :step/math-academy-id 633376 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074832}} {:db/id 17592186074832 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073855 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073575 :question/id #uuid "ca5d9154-4c7e-5866-a6eb-5e4c1fb4d24b" :question/math-academy-id "e-2296"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "76a2f388-bfe6-567b-beec-c59644da1e8a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074484} {:db/id 17592186074523}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Ratios From Tape Diagrams Using Multiple Units"} :step/id #uuid "53d075f6-e5a4-5538-8f53-8f68f0d418a4" :step/math-academy-id 633379}] :activity/title "Tape Diagrams" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186073974} {:db/id 17592186074827 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074969 :tutorial/content "We can illustrate ratios with a **tape diagram**, where each box represents a unit.

curve at the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡xy \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(0,\frac{\pi }{2})={f}_{y}(0,\frac{\pi }{2})i-{f}_{x}(0,\frac{\pi }{2})j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))\,j \\  & =(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))\,j \\ t(0,\frac{\pi }{2}) & =(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-0\operatorname{cos}⁡(0\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}))i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}))j \\  & =-i+\frac{\pi }{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =8xy+2-8e \\ 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy & =2-8e\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=2-8e.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,e)={f}_{y}(1,e)\,i-{f}_{x}(1,e)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{2x}{y}-8x)i-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8y)\,j \\ t(1,e) & =(\frac{2(1)}{e}-8(1))i-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡e-8(e))\,j \\  & =(\frac{2}{e}-8)i+(8e-2)j\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & =3-{x}^{2}-{y}^{3} \\ xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=3.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,-1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-1,-1)={f}_{y}(-1,-1)i-{f}_{x}(-1,-1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3})j \\  & =(x+3{y}^{2})i-(y+2x)j \\ t(-1,-1) & =(-1+3(-1)^{2})i-(-1+2(-1))j \\  & =2\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,2)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-1,2)={f}_{y}(-1,2)i-{f}_{x}(-1,2)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y)j \\  & =(2y-2)i-2x\,j \\ t(-1,2) & =(2(2)-2)i-2(-1)\,j \\  & =2\,i+2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{y}-1 & =xy \\ x{e}^{y}-xy & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}-xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,0)={f}_{y}(1,0)i-{f}_{x}(1,0)j
$$

 

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}-xy)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}-xy)j \\  & =(x{e}^{y}-x)i-({e}^{y}-y)j \\ t(1,0) & =((1){e}^{0}-(1))i-({e}^{0}-(0))j \\  & =-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-j.$"} {:db/id 17592186499554 :question/id #uuid "ea587ab0-d077-5468-b262-1697c88c7094" :question/math-academy-id "q-72389" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e1052d2-3a28-5ca0-9e37-9f2ccf48871c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-i-j" :db/id 17592186498760} {:answer/id #uuid "0f687a71-756e-59f6-bc52-a42d2a1ff16b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-i-3\,j" :db/id 17592186498761} {:answer/id #uuid "1ac23b03-c1ad-5ab7-be63-a35fc34705f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i-3\,j" :db/id 17592186498787} {:answer/id #uuid "5cf883f8-d823-5d14-9a1b-8d3c64093c5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\,i-2\,j" :db/id 17592186498942} {:answer/id #uuid "fac357f6-d241-5f53-aa60-7685a0cfadeb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i-j" :db/id 17592186499292}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498760} :answer-field/id #uuid "0f7da737-6ab6-5dc3-a356-5e38af59041a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499319}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $2{e}^{xy}=x+y+1.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{e}^{xy} & =x+y+1 \\ 2{e}^{xy}-x-y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2{e}^{xy}-x-y-1$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(0,1)={f}_{y}(0,1)\,i-{f}_{x}(0,1)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{e}^{xy}-x-y-1)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{e}^{xy}-x-y-1)\,j \\  & =(2x{e}^{xy}-1)\,i-(2y{e}^{xy}-1)\,j \\ t(0,1) & =(2(0){e}^{(0)(1)}-1)\,i-(2(1){e}^{(0)(1)}-1)\,j \\  & =-i-j\end{aligned}
$$

which points on the curve ${y}^{2}+2xy={x}^{2}+8$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $j?$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

- **I.** $(-2,-2)$
- **II.** $(0,2)$
- **III.** $(1,2)$
- **IV.** $(2,0)$
- **V.** $(2,1)$
- **VI.** $(2,2)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2xy & ={x}^{2}+8 \\ {y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=8.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2})j \\  & =2(y+x)\,i-2(y-x)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j$, we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ (2(y+x)\,i-2(y-x)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -2(y-x) & =0 \\ y & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ (x)^{2}+2x(x)-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=2$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(2,2).$

- If $x=-2$, we get $y=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,-2).$"} {:db/id 17592186339115 :question/id #uuid "5577e429-0d55-5dd4-b588-49ac727edd6b" :question/math-academy-id "q-72440"} {:db/id which points on the curve $2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=-y$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $j?$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

- **I.** $(-1,1)$
- **II.** $(0,0)$
- **III.** $(0,\frac{1}{3})$
- **IV.** $(1,1)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y)\,j \\  & =(-6y+1)\,i-4x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j,$ we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ((-6y+1)\,i-4x\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -4x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=0$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 2({0}^{2})-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 3{y}^{2}-y & =0 \\ y(3y-1) & =0 \\ y & =0,\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the corresponding points are $(0,0)$ and $(0,\frac{1}{3}).$"} {:db/id 17592186375335 :question/id #uuid "703e7046-bcfc-54c8-9bb1-c367d4d9ddb7" :question/math-academy-id "q-72427"} {:db/id 17592186388083 :question/id #uuid "f930a915-2d68-50d6-9185-efb4889fde3f" :question/math-academy-id "q-130209"} {:db/id 17592186400450 :question/id #uuid "6851bbc7-80d6-5dc9-8a00-f559624fa12f" :question/math-academy-id "q-130217"} {:db/id 17592186403571 :question/id #uuid "49dc4b38-854b-53b5-ba44-1bf47c27ef1c" :question/math-academy-id "q-72412" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b3b898a6-e9f5-51f8-8993-b6f0322af5e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(3,2)$ and $(-1,3)$" :db/id 17592186403573} {:answer/id #uuid "3acac861-9675-5531-8e0f-29301bd84beb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$" :db/id 17592186403574} {:answer/id #uuid "879099ba-26c3-5eca-b156-1546984f09e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,2)$ and $(-1,-2)$" :db/id 17592186403575} {:answer/id #uuid "56e7a278-62d5-5448-adb4-7672d93764ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,2)$ and $(1,-2)$" :db/id 17592186403576} {:answer/id #uuid "c66b876c-2af7-5756-8122-0570c4918dbd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,3)$ and $(3,-2)$" :db/id 17592186403577}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186403575} :answer-field/id #uuid "22c59322-d13f-5287-a0fa-c2f86091a95e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186403572}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}-4xy=-5{x}^{2}+1$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4xy & =-5{x}^{2}+1 \\ {y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2})j \\  & =2(y-2x)\,i-(10x-4y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ (2(y-2x)\,i-(10x-4y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2(y-2x) & =0 \\ y & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=2x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ (2x)^{2}-4x(2x)+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ 4{x}^{2}-8{x}^{2}+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=1$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(1,2).$

- If $x=-1$, we get $y=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,-2).$"} {:db/id 17592186447371 :question/id #uuid "2ac861e6-ea7e-53f0-b9c2-bba93cd70561" :question/math-academy-id "q-130227"} {:db/id 17592186447374 :question/id #uuid "caca4712-f17f-5ed4-8f57-6c6c5c27d1ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-130213"} {:db/id 17592186459235 :question/id #uuid "49174b89-3c43-532e-8951-fbe13dc1efa4" :question/math-academy-id "q-130221"} {:db/id 17592186499527 :question/id #uuid "b5a12ff0-24e0-5963-9f16-1e9a01270fba" :question/math-academy-id "q-72439" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b1f9282-40f6-534c-9cb9-df688ee64de0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-2,-1)$ only" :db/id 17592186498822} {:answer/id #uuid "9c2fce83-b1b2-5397-8cab-576be2461576" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,2)$ only" :db/id 17592186499059} {:answer/id #uuid "a70e370b-8012-5ba7-8c81-0ea9db91d6f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,-1)$ only" :db/id 17592186499097} {:answer/id #uuid "d553a226-27d4-508f-a4c8-4c5c6f0cd0cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-2,-1)$  and $(1,2)$" :db/id 17592186499207} {:answer/id #uuid "e67fa0c9-ee34-5eea-a810-dee87b7233d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,-2)$  and $(1,2)$" :db/id 17592186499253}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498822} :answer-field/id #uuid "f38fea1a-0a62-5cc4-9aaa-d50dbb5879df" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499427}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}-xy=x+1$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$

:topic/math-academy-id 1940} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125292 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125733 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the equation of the **tangent line** to the ellipse 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac{y^2}{4} =1
$$

 at the point $P(3,1).$

To solve this problem, we could find the slope of the line using techniques from single-variable calculus. However, we can also solve the problem by computing the gradient of a two-variable function.

Let's start by defining 

$$
f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac {y^2}{4}.
$$

Then, the given ellipse is the level curve  $f(x,y)=1.$

Now, we know that $\nabla \! f(3,1)$ is a vector that's normal to the level curve $f(x,y)= 1$ at $P(3,1).$ So, it's also normal to the tangent line to our ellipse at $P.$

![](images/3d/3dc75e8fd4083af1bf90f46b2e875d5d552bffdc5c1cfaeabebef70f79f00828.png)

Suppose that $(x,y)$ is any point on that tangent line. Then $\mathbf v=\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle$ is a vector that's parallel to the tangent line. So $\mathbf v$ must be also orthogonal to $\nabla f(3,1),$ and since the dot product of two orthogonal vectors is zero, we have that

$$
\nabla f(3,1)\,\cdot \,\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle = 0.
$$

Now, computing $\nabla\! f$ and evaluating it at the point $P(3,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{x}{6},\frac{y}{2}⟩ \\ ∇\,f(3,1) & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the equation of our tangent, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(3,1)\cdot ⟨x-3,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}(x-3)+\frac{1}{2}(y-1) & =0 \\ (x-3)+(y-1) & =0 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7a9dede8-0672-56eb-9084-cf581e3fb05f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2496 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7cc9655e-83bb-5f85-8c20-add1d27fb5e0" :step/math-academy-id 11184 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125464}} {:db/id 17592186125293 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124454 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124258 :question/id #uuid "a01560be-9023-593a-87d3-7412f3b208a3" :question/math-academy-id "e-3362"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5ae7e9c8-60e9-5f5e-afbf-1de6bb01bf07" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050027}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124979} {:db/id 17592186125075} {:db/id 17592186265823} {:db/id 17592186265826} {:db/id 17592186339099} {:db/id 17592186388076} {:db/id 17592186393208} {:db/id 17592186447370} {:db/id 17592186447373} {:db/id 17592186459277}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Tangent Line to a Level Curve"} :step/id #uuid "204027bd-d606-5131-82eb-717c2823cc14" :step/math-academy-id 11185 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125294}} {:db/id 17592186125294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125734 :tutorial/content "Given a level curve $f(x,y) = f(x_0,y_0),$ a **tangent vector** is

$$
\mathbf t(x_0,y_0) = f_y(x_0,y_0) \ \mathbf i - f_x(x_0,y_0) \ \mathbf j.
$$

 

To understand why the above vector is tangent to the level curve, first recall that the gradient vector $\nabla f(x_0,y_0)$ is normal to the level curve. Now, by computing the dot product, we see that the vector $\mathbf t$ is orthogonal to the gradient vector $\nabla\! f{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f\cdot t & =({f}_{x}\text{ }i+{f}_{y}\text{ }j)\cdot ({f}_{y}\text{ }i-{f}_{x}j) \\  & ={f}_{x}{f}_{y}-{f}_{y}{f}_{x} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $\mathbf t$ is tangent to the level curve." :tutorial/id #uuid "6ef07808-783a-543e-9217-5d3d0a9ae13a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2497 :tutorial/title "The Tangent Vector to a Plane :tutorial/content "Now, let's state the previous result more generally.

Let $f(x,y)$ be a function that's continuously differentiable at the point $P(x_0,y_0).$   If  $\nabla f(x_0, y_0)$ is not the zero vector, then it is orthogonal to the tangent line to the level curve

$$
\nabla\! f (x_0,y_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0,y-y_0\rangle  = 0.

$$
f_x(x_0,y_0)(x-x_0) + f_y(x_0,y_0)(y-y_0)   = 0.

11192} {:db/id 17592186125807 :tutorial/content "Now, let's state the previous result more generally.

Let $f(x,y)$ be a function that's continuously differentiable at the point $P(x_0,y_0).$   If  $\nabla f(x_0, y_0)$ is not the zero vector, then it is orthogonal to the tangent line to the level curve 

$$
f(x,y)= f(x_0,y_0)
$$

at the point $P.$ The equation of the tangent can then be written as

$$
\nabla\! f (x_0,y_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0,y-y_0\rangle  = 0.
$$

Writing this explicitly, we get

$$
f_x(x_0,y_0)(x-x_0) + f_y(x_0,y_0)(y-y_0)   = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e9c2ee0b-08cf-5f42-bf09-f80dcd82051d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3866 :tutorial/title "Tangent Line to a Level Curve"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186482621} :activity/id #uuid "12b9dfa6-9b29-5bbc-991a-88ee2275afa9" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049511 :topic/id #uuid "fabe76f4-9f30-5b59-b906-f5fa71cfb89f" :topic/math-academy-id 1940} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186482619 :step/content {:db/id 17592186482608 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "644861a7-1cbc-5867-8185-defe9888db93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i-j" :db/id 17592186482005} {:answer/id #uuid "73996ca2-8d53-576d-9599-e7d064a54b16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\,j" :db/id 17592186482042} {:answer/id #uuid "8054282c-e26d-5511-a066-a463f3020bfe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+2\,j" :db/id 17592186482072} {:answer/id #uuid "b5877c60-a794-5905-b476-5b03a5663061" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-i" :db/id 17592186482203} {:answer/id #uuid "f6a04f0f-fb4c-5c47-a171-0ccaf2eedb86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-i+2\,j" :db/id 17592186482358}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186482072} :answer-field/id #uuid "7ad3bafa-b0de-589d-9a11-64d4563a5603" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186482443}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "eaaccc28-17cb-56b1-b96e-6187ebe91480" :question/math-academy-id "q-130203" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${y}^{2}=1-{x}^{2}+2y.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-1,2).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =1-{x}^{2}+2y \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,2)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-1,2)={f}_{y}(-1,2)i-{f}_{x}(-1,2)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y)j \\  & =(2y-2)i-2x\,j \\ t(-1,2) & =(2(2)-2)i-2(-1)\,j \\  & =2\,i+2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $2\,i+2\,j.$"} :step/id #uuid "02f310c0-3a63-5ca4-a009-b9bb2d7c2097" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482651}} {:db/id 17592186482621 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323918 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18cbb66c-c87e-532e-b215-79cebdd50220" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2e-8)\,i+(\frac{e}{2}-8)j" :db/id 17592186321343} {:answer/id #uuid "25737ab8-5934-517a-82e3-355f226249ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1-4e)\,i+(\frac{2}{e}-8)j" :db/id 17592186321438} {:answer/id #uuid "569fd915-b891-5273-a763-b23c030c775d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2-8e)\,i+(2-8e)j" :db/id 17592186321831} {:answer/id #uuid "91bfacf0-e81a-591f-b5c7-eb843413fffc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{2}{e}-8)i+(8e-2)\,j" :db/id 17592186322304} {:answer/id #uuid "e6c24a19-a0b8-5781-9f03-f3684c7d7f7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(8-2e)\,i+(\frac{8}{e}-2)j" :db/id 17592186322954}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322304} :answer-field/id #uuid "2328f82b-ecf4-5e93-897c-028b4fd16484" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323237}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "12b276e2-b703-55f7-94b8-069326b3f510" :question/math-academy-id "q-37516" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y=8xy+2-8e.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,e).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =8xy+2-8e \\ 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy & =2-8e\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=2-8e.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,e)={f}_{y}(1,e)\,i-{f}_{x}(1,e)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{2x}{y}-8x)i-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8y)\,j \\ t(1,e) & =(\frac{2(1)}{e}-8(1))i-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡e-8(e))\,j \\  & =(\frac{2}{e}-8)i+(8e-2)j\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, our tangent vector is $(\frac{2}{e}-8)i+(8e-2)\,j.$"} :step/id #uuid "05e7d7d3-d815-5b26-b630-27644d17a707" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482641}} {:db/id 17592186482636 :step/content {:db/id 17592186403571 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b3b898a6-e9f5-51f8-8993-b6f0322af5e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(3,2)$ and $(-1,3)$" :db/id 17592186403573} {:answer/id #uuid "3acac861-9675-5531-8e0f-29301bd84beb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$" :db/id 17592186403574} {:answer/id #uuid "879099ba-26c3-5eca-b156-1546984f09e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,2)$ and $(-1,-2)$" :db/id 17592186403575} {:answer/id #uuid "56e7a278-62d5-5448-adb4-7672d93764ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,2)$ and $(1,-2)$" :db/id 17592186403576} {:answer/id #uuid "c66b876c-2af7-5756-8122-0570c4918dbd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,3)$ and $(3,-2)$" :db/id 17592186403577}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186403575} :answer-field/id #uuid "22c59322-d13f-5287-a0fa-c2f86091a95e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186403572}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "49dc4b38-854b-53b5-ba44-1bf47c27ef1c" :question/math-academy-id "q-72412" :question/problem "At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}-4xy=-5{x}^{2}+1$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4xy & =-5{x}^{2}+1 \\ {y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2})j \\  & =2(y-2x)\,i-(10x-4y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ (2(y-2x)\,i-(10x-4y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2(y-2x) & =0 \\ y & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=2x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ (2x)^{2}-4x(2x)+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ 4{x}^{2}-8{x}^{2}+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=1$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(1,2).$

- If $x=-1$, we get $y=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,-2).$"} :step/id #uuid "6e92b42c-037c-5e2c-9313-5354ee48f332" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482619}} {:db/id 17592186482641 :step/content "9c0801c9-8ff6-5c1f-a200-5a0877707694" :question/math-academy-id "q-72410" :question/problem "At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}+2xy={x}^{2}+8$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $j?$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

- **I.** $(-2,-2)$
- **II.** $(0,2)$
- **III.** $(1,2)$
- **IV.** $(2,0)$
- **V.** $(2,1)$
- **VI.** $(2,2)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2xy & ={x}^{2}+8 \\ {y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=8.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2})j \\  & =2(y+x)\,i-2(y-x)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j$, we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ (2(y+x)\,i-2(y-x)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -2(y-x) & =0 \\ y & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ (x)^{2}+2x(x)-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=2$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(2,2).$

- If $x=-2$, we get $y=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,-2).$"} :step/id #uuid "8010488e-cbf0-5349-af76-b70ec53c1a3b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482636}} {:db/id 17592186482651 :step/content :question/math-academy-id "q-130225" :question/problem "At which points on the curve $2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=-y$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $j?$

- **II.** $(0,0)$
- **III.** $(0,\frac{1}{3})$
- **IV.** $(1,1)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y)\,j \\  & =(-6y+1)\,i-4x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j,$ we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ((-6y+1)\,i-4x\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -4x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=0$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 2({0}^{2})-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 3{y}^{2}-y & =0 \\ y(3y-1) & =0 \\ y & =0,\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the corresponding points are $(0,0)$ and $(0,\frac{1}{3}).$"} :step/id #uuid "d3f5afa9-3e2d-58c5-8c55-a63599bc185e"}] :activity/title "Tangent Lines to Level Curves" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186481766} {:db/id 17592186482621 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323918 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18cbb66c-c87e-532e-b215-79cebdd50220" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2e-8)\,i+(\frac{e}{2}-8)j" :db/id 17592186321343} {:answer/id #uuid "25737ab8-5934-517a-82e3-355f226249ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1-4e)\,i+(\frac{2}{e}-8)j" :db/id 17592186321438} {:answer/id #uuid "569fd915-b891-5273-a763-b23c030c775d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2-8e)\,i+(2-8e)j" :db/id 17592186321831} {:answer/id #uuid "91bfacf0-e81a-591f-b5c7-eb843413fffc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{2}{e}-8)i+(8e-2)\,j" :db/id 17592186322304} {:answer/id #uuid "e6c24a19-a0b8-5781-9f03-f3684c7d7f7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(8-2e)\,i+(\frac{8}{e}-2)j" :db/id 17592186322954}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322304} :answer-field/id #uuid "2328f82b-ecf4-5e93-897c-028b4fd16484" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323237}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "12b276e2-b703-55f7-94b8-069326b3f510" :question/math-academy-id "q-37516" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y=8xy+2-8e.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,e).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =8xy+2-8e \\ 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy & =2-8e\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=2-8e.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,e)={f}_{y}(1,e)\,i-{f}_{x}(1,e)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{2x}{y}-8x)i-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8y)\,j \\ t(1,e) & =(\frac{2(1)}{e}-8(1))i-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡e-8(e))\,j \\  & =(\frac{2}{e}-8)i+(8e-2)j\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$

$$
t(-1,2)={f}_{y}(-1,2)i-{f}_{x}(-1,2)j

$$

$$

vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $j?$

- **I.** $(-2,-2)$
- **II.** $(0,2)$
- **III.** $(1,2)$
- **IV.** $(2,0)$
- **V.** $(2,1)$
- **VI.** $(2,2)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2xy & ={x}^{2}+8 \\ {y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=8.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2})j \\  & =2(y+x)\,i-2(y-x)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j$, we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ (2(y+x)\,i-2(y-x)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -2(y-x) & =0 \\ y & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ (x)^{2}+2x(x)-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=2$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(2,2).$

- If $x=-2$, we get $y=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,-2).$"} :step/id #uuid "8010488e-cbf0-5349-af76-b70ec53c1a3b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482636}} {:db/id 17592186482636 :step/content {:db/id 17592186403571 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b3b898a6-e9f5-51f8-8993-b6f0322af5e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(3,2)$ and $(-1,3)$" :db/id 17592186403573} {:answer/id #uuid "3acac861-9675-5531-8e0f-29301bd84beb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$" :db/id 17592186403574} {:answer/id #uuid "879099ba-26c3-5eca-b156-1546984f09e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,2)$ and $(-1,-2)$" :db/id 17592186403575} {:answer/id #uuid "56e7a278-62d5-5448-adb4-7672d93764ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,2)$ and $(1,-2)$" :db/id 17592186403576} {:answer/id #uuid "c66b876c-2af7-5756-8122-0570c4918dbd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,3)$ and $(3,-2)$" :db/id 17592186403577}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186403575} :answer-field/id #uuid "22c59322-d13f-5287-a0fa-c2f86091a95e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186403572}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "49dc4b38-854b-53b5-ba44-1bf47c27ef1c" :question/math-academy-id "q-72412" :question/problem "At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}-4xy=-5{x}^{2}+1$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2})j \\  & =2(y-2x)\,i-(10x-4y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ (2(y-2x)\,i-(10x-4y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2(y-2x) & =0 \\ y & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=2x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ (2x)^{2}-4x(2x)+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ 4{x}^{2}-8{x}^{2}+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=1$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(1,2).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-xy & =x+1 \\ {y}^{2}-xy-x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-xy-x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-xy-x)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-xy-x)j \\  & =(2y-x)\,i+(y+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((2y-x)\,i+(y+1)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2y-x & =0 \\ x & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=2y$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-(2y)y-(2y) & =1 \\ {y}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-2y-1 & =0 \\ -{y}^{2}-2y-1 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}+2y+1 & =0 \\ (y+1)^{2} & =0 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $y=-1$, we get $x=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,-1).$"} :step/id #uuid "2f4293a9-a10e-5b28-82a5-1a8b2fd293b4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186499584}} {:db/id 17592186499584 :step/content {:db/id 17592186363031 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29f3795a-9c5d-564b-99c5-8234a8f8adae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\,j" :db/id 17592186363033} {:answer/id #uuid "17117ea5-c48d-5a75-87dd-44fd4b306516" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "i-2\,j" :db/id 17592186363034} {:answer/id #uuid "a1a1d040-84f6-5093-b8b7-a02c512a3ef2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\,i-2\,j" :db/id 17592186363035} {:answer/id #uuid "afb47ff5-03cb-5158-9e15-6ff6eeca5436" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\,i" :db/id 17592186363036} {:answer/id #uuid "0c788786-b66b-5944-b4ad-21c56064f8a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+3\,j" :db/id 17592186363037}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186363037} :answer-field/id #uuid "d07c4d10-4f15-5f81-9aca-9c05aa1a4821" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186363032}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "55fb49e6-3301-5747-997a-6aea4f919a61" :question/math-academy-id "q-130201" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $xy=3-{x}^{2}-{y}^{3}.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-1,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & =3-{x}^{2}-{y}^{3} \\ xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=3.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,-1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-1,-1)={f}_{y}(-1,-1)i-{f}_{x}(-1,-1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{3})j \\  & =(x+3{y}^{2})i-(y+2x)j \\ t(-1,-1) & =(-1+3(-1)^{2})i-(-1+2(-1))j \\  & =2\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}-xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,0)={f}_{y}(1,0)i-{f}_{x}(1,0)j
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-xy & =x+1 \\ {y}^{2}-xy-x & =1\end{aligned}

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-xy-x)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-xy-x)j \\  & =(2y-x)\,i+(y+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((2y-x)\,i+(y+1)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2y-x & =0 \\ x & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-(2y)y-(2y) & =1 \\ {y}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-2y-1 & =0 \\ -{y}^{2}-2y-1 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}+2y+1 & =0 \\ (y+1)^{2} & =0 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the system $Ax=b$, where the matrix $A$ and the vector $b$ are shown below. Given that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, find the minimum value of $‖Ax-b‖.$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 14 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 14 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}} \\ Ax & =b\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 14 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}15 \\ 15\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{15}[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}15 \\ 15\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The minimum value of $‖Ax-b‖$ is attained when $x=\overset{^}{x},$ which is the least-squares solution of the system $Ax=b.$ In this case, $A\overset{^}{x}$ represents the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space of $A,$ and $‖A\overset{^}{x}-b‖$ is the distance between the vector $b$ and the column space. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}A\overset{^}{x}-b & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 14 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -4 \\ -8 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
‖A\overset{^}{x}-b‖=\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(-8)^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{110}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186354440 :question/id #uuid "8fe94dab-ed8a-5caf-8874-c5b5c72bebb6" :question/math-academy-id "q-85909"} {:db/id 17592186365066 :question/id #uuid 17592186134695 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135059 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-2 \\ -{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=4 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

It is easy to show that the system is inconsistent (i.e., it has no solution). However, in real-world problems, we might want to find an approximate solution to the system. 

Let's formulate the problem a little more rigorously. Firstly, we write down the system in the form $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\mathbin{:}$
![](images/22/22b8abd4638e579875755f482442cf1dbf89653bd9d396b4a802217e25177839.svg)

We are interested in vectors $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ such that $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is very close to $\mathbf b.$ More precisely, we wish to *minimize the distance* between $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and $\mathbf b.$ Recall that the distance between $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and $\mathbf b$ is given by

$$
\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert.
$$

The smaller the value of $\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert,$ the better our approximation $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ will be. 

In terms of vector subspaces, we wish to find a vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ that lies in $\textrm{Col}(A)$ and is closest to $\mathbf{b}.$
Therefore, $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ must be the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$

![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png)

It can be shown that ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is found by solving the corresponding **normal equation**, given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

We'll prove this at the end of the lesson. Note that the normal equation is obtained by left-multiplying the equation $A {\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf b$ by $A^T.$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix $A^T \! A$ is invertible. Therefore, left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T \! A)^{-1},$ we obtain

$$
{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = (A^T \! A)^{-1}A^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

We now compute the right-hand side as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -4 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 18\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{99}[\begin{aligned}18 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{33} \\ -\frac{38}{33}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is called the **least-squares solution** of the given system.

**Watch out!** We assumed that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, which guarantees that $A^T \! A\,$ is invertible. However, if the columns of $A$ are linearly *dependent,* then we have to use a different approach to solve the problem." :tutorial/id #uuid "548ecdec-2401-51e1-b2cf-d63f0b5a595d" $$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3(x+y)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =3{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3{z}^{2}+1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=3{z}^{2}+1.$"} {:db/id 17592186244158 :question/id #uuid "0fcc97e4-3645-5517-967a-e3b54a04fc40" :question/math-academy-id "q-108744"} {:db/id 17592186244159 :question/id #uuid 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{9x-3y}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|g(x,y)|=y+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{3(3x-y)}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=3x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{3z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{9z-2}{3z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3z}{9z-2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{3z}{9z-2}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\int (1+\frac{2}{9z-2})\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}(z+\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|9z-2|) & =x+K \\ z+\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|9z-2| & =3x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-y+\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|27x-9y-2| & =3x+C \\ \frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|27x-9y-2| & =y+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=27x-9y-2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186275247 :question/id #uuid "282836bd-3e6d-5985-8015-1e73c28407a8" :question/math-academy-id "q-149756"} {:db/id 17592186488190 :question/id #uuid :step/math-academy-id 33755} {:db/id 17592186176758 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177006 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given a differential equation of the form

$$
y' = F(x,y).
$$

By factoring the function $F(x,y),$ we can often convert this differential equation to one that is of the form 

$$
y' = f ( a x + b y ),
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are real constants. Then, using the substitution $z= ax+by,$ we can convert the equation to a separable differential equation. 

To illustrate, let's consider the differential equation

$$
y'  = 9x^2 - 6xy + y^2.
$$

Notice that the right-hand side is a perfect square. So, we factor it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=(3x-y)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z = 3x - y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} = 3 - \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} 
\quad \Rightarrow\quad 
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = 3 - \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

Therefore, we can write our equation in terms of $z$ as

$$
3 - \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} = z^2,
$$

which simplifies to

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}   = 3-z^2.
$$

We now have a separable differential equation." :tutorial/id #uuid "d8aada75-8774-521d-9c38-9a755e683eb4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5510 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "93b65588-48dd-56d7-a249-1757dc172974" :step/math-academy-id 34318 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176726}}] :activity/title "Further Solving First-Order ODEs by Substitution" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176146} {:db/id 17592186176758 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177006 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given a differential equation of the form

$$
f(x)=\frac{2{e}^{x}}{(1+{e}^{x})^{3}},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

find the cumulative distribution function $F(x).$" :question/worked-solution "The cumulative distribution function of a continuous random variable $X$ is the function $F(x)$ defined by

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{2{e}^{t}}{(1+{e}^{t})^{3}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={-\frac{1}{(1+{e}^{t})^{2}}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(1+{e}^{x})^{2}}+1 \\  & =1-\frac{1}{(1+{e}^{x})^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186419956 :question/id #uuid "dbdaccde-7824-5d29-93f1-f05b495a99f8" :question/math-academy-id "q-126213"} {:db/id 17592186419958 :question/id #uuid :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186424884}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|x/3|}}{6},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186442323 :question/id #uuid "7e1280de-34a4-5310-b0ea-3ca5ec3ba975" :question/math-academy-id "q-210763" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "65441b2f-7b3a-53c5-af33-45bf0ced0a21" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{2}" :db/id 17592186442310}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442310} :answer-field/id #uuid "60abe397-ada8-52f7-89c3-1ccbe2f29023" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186442320}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$

$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{5t}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{5x}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{5x}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-5t}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-5t}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$

:answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424883}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{9}(x-1)(x-4),\, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<1 \\ h(x),\, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1,\, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $1\le x\le 4,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ {\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4\end{aligned}
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{x}-\frac{2}{9}(t-1)(t-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{x}-\frac{2}{9}({t}^{2}-5t+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(-\frac{2}{27}{t}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{t}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}t)|}_{1}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x-(-\frac{2}{27}+\frac{5}{9}-\frac{8}{9}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ -\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186442324 :question/id #uuid "990f1bb6-e595-59df-8c02-d323344bc3ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-210785" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133728 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "eedcfa3d-b02b-5f96-99f4-cd0a452d272a" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a CDF Given a PDF With Lower and Upper Bounds"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "da4529e7-604e-506b-adaa-ff85312c20f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{-x^{2}+8x-7}{9}" :db/id 17592186442316}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "da4529e7-604e-506b-adaa-ff85312c20f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{-x^{2}+8x-7}{9}" :db/id 17592186442316} :answer-field/id #uuid "45ff772f-b783-5f66-89ac-69df3d1d8f2a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186442319}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ {\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4\end{aligned}
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{x}(-\frac{2}{9}t+\frac{8}{9})\,\text{d}t \\ \text{ } & ={(-\frac{1}{9}{t}^{2}+\frac{8}{9}t)|}_{1}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}{x}^{2}+\frac{8}{9}x-\frac{7}{9} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}({x}^{2}-8x+7) \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}(x-1)(x-7).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186442325 :question/id #uuid "e65ef0d7-6649-5f56-9e79-7407f7595f66" :question/math-academy-id "q-89621" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c66a62f-9a33-540e-bb1b-485e50f03db9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{256}" :db/id 17592186442303} {:answer/id #uuid "12f66496-4995-5d37-a001-943fa360d144" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{5{x}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{64}" :db/id 17592186442305} {:answer/id #uuid "5de59784-191d-59f0-ab4e-cb2aafa6fe90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{256}" :db/id 17592186442309} {:answer/id #uuid "7295486c-b630-5ce0-8356-5ab47719adad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{256}" :db/id 17592186442311} {:answer/id #uuid "af97dd8a-6b84-534d-9a5b-b7c3f09bac24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{256}" :db/id 17592186442313}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442309} :answer-field/id #uuid "d0e871fb-e944-567c-b4fe-9835a0a9327f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186442321}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186133729 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133519 :question/id #uuid "707e3b49-9c13-50d8-8a7f-c4d5ec44e0ff" :question/math-academy-id "e-13365"} :knowledge-point/id 17592186134578 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135186 :tutorial/content "The cumulative distribution function (or CDF) of a continuous random variable is defined the same way as for a discrete random variable. 

Given a continuous random variable $X,$ the CDF is the function $F(x)$ such that

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x).
$$

If our random variable has the probability density function (or PDF) $f(x),$ then we have

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t) \, \textrm dt.
$$

Note that we use $f(t)dt$ in the integrand because $x$ serves as the upper limit of integration. 

For example, consider the random variable $X$ with the following PDF:

![](images/e7/e79c230f2b548c9280425f555f6d99a8f997e989289a05fb5f4584b656c4dcc8.svg)

Since $f(x)= 0$ for all $x < 0,$  we have

$$
F(x)  = \int_{-\infty}^x 0 \, \textrm dt = 0
$$

if $x<0.$

To compute the CDF for $x\geq 0,$  we integrate $f(x)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =0+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{2}{\pi (1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡t|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡x-\frac{2}{\pi }(0) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing our CDF as a function defined over the entire real line, we get

![](images/66/66b7bf54271075ae72fcf07fa4dc8573a94e97c2b2cc77680c0ec94b6053f360.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "de1bbdf6-687d-537a-a6fe-03d9fafbe841" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8364 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3f773be7-dfa4-524f-aec7-8ade124c5cea" :step/math-academy-id 132590 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134579}} {:db/id 17592186134579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133726 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133516 :question/id #uuid "38b4473a-f956-5af5-863b-387dc10b4924" :question/math-academy-id "e-13362"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1d7509fa-a254-5b78-b307-3e0c4ef4d9ec" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049638}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134158} {:db/id 17592186134538} {:db/id 17592186419947} {:db/id 17592186419952} {:db/id 17592186419953} {:db/id 17592186424144} {:db/id 17592186424145}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a CDF Given a PDF With a Lower Bound"} :step/id #uuid "2411aa47-0b30-5e9c-b541-4d44b5f7aeed" :step/math-academy-id 132591 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134580}} {:db/id 17592186134580 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133727 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133517 :question/id #uuid "98dd834c-ac74-5cdd-88ee-060fd9ac689d" :question/math-academy-id "e-13363"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7b0ce833-e045-5aff-94a4-f9ad56cdb904" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134159} {:db/id 17592186134541} {:db/id 17592186419950} {:db/id 17592186419951} {:db/id 17592186419956} {:db/id 17592186419958} {:db/id 17592186424886} {:db/id 17592186442323}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a CDF Given a PDF That’s Nonzero Over All Real Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "f242a3a5-626f-54b6-b0cc-b8af4506a3f0" :step/math-academy-id 132594 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134581}} {:db/id 17592186134581 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135187 :tutorial/content "When a random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive on the interval $a \leq x \leq b$ only, we have

- $P(X \leq x) = 0$ for $x < a,$ and

- $P(X \leq x) = 1$ for $x > b.$

In these cases, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

![](images/7a/7a64bac7c252a3f52fc92f6364edb5c66f31e47da28e78eeb0d069d894135700.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "0794419f-6b72-568b-a787-d71121c8bcd9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8365 :tutorial/title "Finding a CDF Given a PDF With Lower and Upper Bounds"} :step/id #uuid "a74ce991-870f-5bfa-8a96-8bbed06ce5b6" :step/math-academy-id 132597 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134582}} {:db/id 17592186134582 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133728 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133518 :question/id #uuid "4159a407-ea9f-5728-b219-bf1afab732a2" :question/math-academy-id "e-13364"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "eedcfa3d-b02b-5f96-99f4-cd0a452d272a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134150} {:db/id 17592186134160} {:db/id 17592186419943} {:db/id 17592186419949} {:db/id 17592186419954} {:db/id 17592186419955} {:db/id 17592186424143} {:db/id 17592186424888} {:db/id 17592186442324} {:db/id 17592186442325}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a CDF Given a PDF With Lower and Upper Bounds"} :step/id #uuid "47bc1334-f06b-5cc0-b191-427d1d862db4" :step/math-academy-id 132598 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134583}} {:db/id 17592186134583 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135188 :tutorial/content "As with discrete random variables, we can use the CDF of a continuous random variable to quickly compute a probability over an interval:

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a)
$$

For example, suppose that a random variable $X$ has the following CDF:

$$
F(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}, \qquad -\infty < x < \infty.
$$

We can use the above CDF to quickly compute $P(0 \leq x \leq 1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0\le x\le 1) & =F(1)-F(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-1}}-\frac{1}{1+{e}^{0}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-1}}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & ≈0.231\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that for continuous random variables, it doesn't matter whether or not we include the endpoints of the interval, so we have

$$
P(0 \leq X \leq 1) = P(0 < X \leq 1) = P(0 \leq X < 1) = P(0 < X < 1) = 0.231.
$$

In general, for a continuous random variable $X,$ we have

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b) = P(a < X < b) = F(b) - F(a).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e5203710-822b-55d4-9dfb-985bc4d41d6a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8366 :tutorial/title "Using a CDF to Compute a Probability Over an Interval"} :step/id #uuid "55418ca8-74f9-5755-9f75-2d411c4a476e" :step/math-academy-id 132601 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134584}} {:db/id 17592186134584 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133729 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133519 :question/id #uuid "707e3b49-9c13-50d8-8a7f-c4d5ec44e0ff" :question/math-academy-id "e-13365"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3cbc399b-90f3-5acd-ac70-7345a8436978" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134539} {:db/id 17592186134540} {:db/id 17592186419944} {:db/id 17592186419945} {:db/id 17592186419946} {:db/id 17592186419948} {:db/id 17592186419957} {:db/id 17592186424146} {:db/id 17592186424147} {:db/id 17592186424887} {:db/id 17592186442322}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Probability Over an Interval Using a CDF"} :step/id #uuid "681dc276-df96-5b4d-b26c-338d9da62b88" :step/math-academy-id 132602}] :activity/title "Cumulative Distribution Functions for Continuous Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134025} {:db/id 17592186134578 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135186 :tutorial/content "The cumulative distribution function (or CDF) of a continuous random variable is defined the same way as for a discrete random variable.

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a)
$$

For example, suppose that a random variable $X$ has the following CDF:

$$
F(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}, \qquad -\infty < x < \infty.
$$

We can use the above CDF to quickly compute $P(0 \leq x \leq 1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0\le x\le 1) & =F(1)-F(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-1}}-\frac{1}{1+{e}^{0}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-1}}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & ≈0.231\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that for continuous random variables, it doesn't matter whether or not we include the endpoints of the interval, so we have

$$
P(0 \leq X \leq 1) = P(0 < X \leq 1) = P(0 \leq X < 1) = P(0 < X < 1) = 0.231.
$$

In general, for a continuous random variable $X,$ we have

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b) = P(a < X < b) = F(b) - F(a).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e5203710-822b-55d4-9dfb-985bc4d41d6a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8366 :tutorial/title "Using a CDF to Compute a Probability Over an Interval"} :step/id #uuid "55418ca8-74f9-5755-9f75-2d411c4a476e" :step/math-academy-id 132601 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134584}} {:db/id 17592186135188 :tutorial/content "As with discrete random variables, we can use the CDF of a continuous random variable to quickly compute a probability over an interval:
