17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2b70eaac-0c45-5da5-8a2f-2002d9071035" :question/math-academy-id "q-89727" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|x/3|}}{6},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3f2429d9-8a43-540c-8ee1-21b8c07473a4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186424890}} {:db/id 17592186424890 :step/content {:db/id 17592186424888 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27f33f1e-6e04-5ef0-8a18-a9a9635e495a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}" :db/id 17592186424869} {:answer/id #uuid "7bc40166-55c4-53b3-bf06-562cddc8e868" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}" :db/id 17592186424875} {:answer/id #uuid "8a0df617-e565-5181-bd27-09321bb7abfd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186424877} {:answer/id #uuid "a3e9b386-cf97-5734-82c8-f8b9318ea865" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186424878} {:answer/id #uuid "fbbc1dbf-3cbe-5835-99b1-f9050b0ed224" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{27}{x}^{3}-\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}+\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186424882}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424875} :answer-field/id #uuid "5340e926-2580-5f2f-bf08-46d25e342346" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424883}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "97c91681-ff70-5452-bbfe-e1a92bb2e9d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-126156" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{9}(x-1)(x-4),\, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<1 \\ h(x),\, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1,\, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $1\le x\le 4,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ {\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4\end{aligned}
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{x}-\frac{2}{9}(t-1)(t-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{x}-\frac{2}{9}({t}^{2}-5t+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(-\frac{2}{27}{t}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{t}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}t)|}_{1}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x-(-\frac{2}{27}+\frac{5}{9}-\frac{8}{9}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ -\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9bf4404a-eca3-5f58-9aa8-59a46fdb29aa"} {:db/id 17592186424891 :step/content {:db/id 17592186424887 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d43dadc-2415-595b-83bd-07293e62a4d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186424868} {:answer/id #uuid "2d728c61-ee7a-5242-b976-dff68318b24a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/id 17592186424870} {:answer/id #uuid "54302da3-4ffd-5ae6-9474-e5f95bb705f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186424874} {:answer/id #uuid "86635ef4-b567-5842-a8be-7564b4bc47cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186424876} {:answer/id #uuid "c53339f9-decf-5456-b59e-339275bad539" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}" :db/id 17592186424879}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424870} :answer-field/id #uuid "cf2e7998-6dc3-5838-ae14-0d427c2b4449" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424885}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5d72a8e6-eda0-59be-829b-e0298d5412e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-89695" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the cumulative distribution function

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{64}x(16-{x}^{2}),\, & 0\le x\le 4 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & 0\le x\le 4 \\ 1,\, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability density function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $0<x<4,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & 0\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4\end{aligned}
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{1}{64}t(16-{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{1}{64}(8{t}^{2}-\frac{{t}^{4}}{4})|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{64}(8{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{256}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{256}, & 0\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "443e51e5-e403-51ae-bbff-e563149f49e5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442326}} {:db/id 17592186442328 :step/content {:db/id 17592186442324 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "da4529e7-604e-506b-adaa-ff85312c20f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{-x^{2}+8x-7}{9}" :db/id 17592186442316}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442316} :answer-field/id #uuid "45ff772f-b783-5f66-89ac-69df3d1d8f2a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186442319}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "990f1bb6-e595-59df-8c02-d323344bc3ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-210785" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{9}x+\frac{8}{9},\, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$

$$

where $h(x)=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $1\le x\le 4,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{x}(-\frac{2}{9}t+\frac{8}{9})\,\text{d}t \\ \text{ } & ={(-\frac{1}{9}{t}^{2}+\frac{8}{9}t)|}_{1}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}{x}^{2}+\frac{8}{9}x-\frac{7}{9} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}({x}^{2}-8x+7) \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}(x-1)(x-7).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "7a43148a-546c-5e25-817d-f6a542bfe3c4"} {:db/id 17592186442329 :step/content {:db/id 17592186134539 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a96b44b4-1f7e-576d-9e77-9ec278a83d36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186133273} {:answer/id #uuid "107b6d59-d74b-5f3c-9bc5-01a9d06b20b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{e}" :db/id 17592186133276} {:answer/id #uuid "105177ed-381e-5551-8d54-f794cc7ae2f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186442304} {:answer/id #uuid "c6834059-6614-531c-86f9-081bd2ed69b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186442314} {:answer/id #uuid "f7ff0cb6-5ee6-5486-95b5-ba7fabd16b87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{1}{e}" :db/id 17592186442317}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442304} :answer-field/id #uuid "d3fece95-8a02-51e6-a7b8-03ddf8d52dc7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186133272}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d416c744-adfb-5c13-80ec-0e124bb7f438" :question/math-academy-id "q-89139" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the cumulative distribution function

$$

find $P(X>2).$" :question/worked-solution "We can perform this computation using the complement, as follows:

$$
f(x)=\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-|5x|},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{5x}}{2},\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

where $h(x)=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-5t}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{5t}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{5x}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{5x}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-5t}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-5t}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-5t}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{5x}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cdf24c85-fec2-557e-990a-b96c38922ff0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442328}}] :activity/title "Cumulative Distribution Functions for Continuous Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186442302} {:db/id 17592186442329 :step/content {:db/id 17592186134539 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a96b44b4-1f7e-576d-9e77-9ec278a83d36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186133273} {:answer/id #uuid "107b6d59-d74b-5f3c-9bc5-01a9d06b20b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{e}" :db/id 17592186133276} {:answer/id #uuid "105177ed-381e-5551-8d54-f794cc7ae2f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186442304} {:answer/id #uuid "c6834059-6614-531c-86f9-081bd2ed69b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186442314} {:answer/id #uuid "f7ff0cb6-5ee6-5486-95b5-ba7fabd16b87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{1}{e}" :db/id 17592186442317}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442304} :answer-field/id #uuid "d3fece95-8a02-51e6-a7b8-03ddf8d52dc7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186133272}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d416c744-adfb-5c13-80ec-0e124bb7f438" :question/math-academy-id "q-89139" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the cumulative distribution function

random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-|5x|},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{5x}}{2},\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

where $h(x)=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-5t}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{5t}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{5x}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{5x}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-5t}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-5t}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-5t}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{5x}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-5x}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cdf24c85-fec2-557e-990a-b96c38922ff0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442328}} {:db/id 17592186442327 :step/content {:db/id 17592186442325 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c66a62f-9a33-540e-bb1b-485e50f03db9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{256}" :db/id 17592186442303} {:answer/id #uuid "12f66496-4995-5d37-a001-943fa360d144" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{5{x}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{64}" :db/id 17592186442305} {:answer/id #uuid "5de59784-191d-59f0-ab4e-cb2aafa6fe90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{256}" :db/id 17592186442309} {:answer/id #uuid "7295486c-b630-5ce0-8356-5ab47719adad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{256}" :db/id 17592186442311} {:answer/id #uuid "af97dd8a-6b84-534d-9a5b-b7c3f09bac24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{256}" :db/id 17592186442313}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442309} :answer-field/id #uuid "d0e871fb-e944-567c-b4fe-9835a0a9327f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186442321}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e65ef0d7-6649-5f56-9e79-7407f7595f66" :question/math-academy-id "q-89621" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability density function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $0<x<4,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$

$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$

$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{256}, & 0\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "443e51e5-e403-51ae-bbff-e563149f49e5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442326}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c66a62f-9a33-540e-bb1b-485e50f03db9" :answer/type {:db/id If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}$, where ${a}_{2}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}.$ 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 4 \\ -2 & -6 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we reduce the matrix $A$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 4 \\ -2 & -6 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 13\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{13}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-4){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $3$rd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(A)$ is $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{3}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $2$nd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${a}_{2}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{{(0)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{3}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}=3\cdot 0=0.$"} {:db/id 17592186247221 :question/id #uuid "1560ce17-f00a-5fcc-81e8-d48fb2971bfa" :question/math-academy-id "q-111468"} {:db/id 17592186247222 ![](images/84/84cdf6af82bd0d301ca50b1c7c41bccbd0a3cfb42be17bc84ec2f12e46032161.svg)

Therefore, we can write

![](images/22/22d4eb11af0168d4fabc8b3ebbe1befd24620db11b6a31709472ba91bb1ed794.svg)

The vector $\mathbf{a}_3$ was not included in the basis because the $3$rd column of $A$ was not a pivot column. This means that $\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$

![](images/f3/f3f4e0d48c58be10684eada3fd320001dc056f2d1070707d9443c9533b7b5e35.svg)

![](images/cf/cf66dc341420f6c399e1ad7e108986505cb349d3aba1aeaacee636e7b6ec4b94.svg)

If we reduced this matrix to the *reduced* row echelon form, we get

![](images/84/847a4dd2e37e6e577bd9a38160f03bcb5839fbf617d76ebe0a2b42cdba0ebce1.svg)

Finally, the third column of the *reduced* matrix tells us that $x_1=3$ and $x_2=-2,$ meaning that
![](images/18/1892b80eb017795a7420b59053b836bea894ff77b7478fc7f884de6b43384cb1.svg)

In general, if the $n$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express $\mathbf{a}_n$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix.

W=[\begin{aligned}3 & -9 & 6 \\ -5 & 15 & 10\end{aligned}]

$$

$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $3$rd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(W)$ is $\{{w}_{1},{w}_{3}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 10\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $2$nd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${w}_{2}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 15\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{w}_{2}}={{(-3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{w}_{1}}+{{(0)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{3}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 10\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{w}_{3}}.
$$

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we reduce the matrix $P$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 2 & 0 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(P)$ is $\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $4$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${p}_{4}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{10}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} {:db/id 17592186381985 :question/id #uuid "8d1f0a35-56cb-5370-99fa-b599f7ccb0a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-363840"} {:db/id 17592186408019 :question/id #uuid - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{5} \\ 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423863 :question/id #uuid "bd607d3f-88f1-5057-a261-73a39b9023d2" :question/math-academy-id "q-363834"} {:db/id 17592186430360 :question/id #uuid - $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$"} {:db/id 17592186443407 :question/id #uuid "c1d729e8-d1cb-584b-b25e-2da8d463c255" :question/math-academy-id "q-363831" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid </table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} {:db/id 17592186443408 :question/id #uuid "dd93c01d-3a4b-5e26-802f-bf34131bc696" :question/math-academy-id "q-363664" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid </table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{x}_{2}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & 0 & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162043 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161837 :question/id #uuid "4fd6d412-d080-5fd1-9318-65a0f5f02dc6" :question/math-academy-id "e-8634"} :knowledge-point/id - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{6}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162725 :question/id #uuid "dcd0e8b8-71e5-5dcd-a370-0847d15e9434" :question/math-academy-id "q-98797"} {:db/id 17592186371422 :question/id #uuid "fd52405b-2747-5b7b-9ac8-728557a18405" :question/math-academy-id "q-98769" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "65acaa42-33cd-5757-90f9-4d51036d283f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186371424} {:answer/id #uuid "c9e77905-5ec8-56d5-8779-68fa5b781883" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186371425} {:answer/id #uuid "97daab37-f8ae-5701-b85b-b2e30894a4f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186371426} {:answer/id #uuid "b4e0b9ef-caf7-5749-a8a6-77538e234c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186371427} {:answer/id #uuid "a5fd5a22-26d6-55d8-a7db-98cfc7d4ab6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186371428}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186371426} :answer-field/id #uuid "89ed90b3-a22c-5487-9e5f-dfdcd163748b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186371423}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

$$

$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]

such that 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.

$$

$$

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

$$

$$

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

</table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{3}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} \\ 2\sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]-\frac{2}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048654} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "223c8e67-5171-5ea9-813f-ad2c34f62661" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value singular value decomposition (SVD) of any matrix! The algorithm for computing an SVD of a rectangular $m\times n$ matrix $(m\neq n)$ is similar to the algorithm for square matrices.

As an example, let's consider the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/f6/f65e0eee905da85ce0be4bbf39546c2b31c2bac082ff00a6a1d54fd5b89a4a4e.svg)

Notice that $A$ is a ${\color{blue}{3}}\times {\color{red}{2}}$ matrix. So, to compute the SVD of $A,$ we must write

$$
A=U \Sigma V^T,
$$

where

- $\Sigma$ is a ${\color{blue}{3}}\times {\color{red}{2}}$ matrix with the singular values of $A$ (ordered from largest to smallest) on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal ${\color{blue}{3}} \times {\color{blue}{3}}$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal ${\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{red}{2}}$ matrix.

We proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.**  Find the singular values of $A.$ Computing the eigenvalues of $A^TA,$ we get

$$
\lambda_1 = 4, \qquad \lambda_2 = 2.
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are 

$$
\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1} =  2,  \qquad \sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2} =  \sqrt{2}.
$$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$). Seeking non-zero solutions of $(A^T \! A - \lambda_1 I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ and $(A^T \! A - \lambda_2 I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvectors 
![](images/07/07085f021218ff17060b3c1a9099e1cabad24b3d12269f97f1fe50d49b970f6b.svg)

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A.$ Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the first two columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\mathbf u_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute $\mathbf u_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $U$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix. However, we do not have the third singular value, so we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 
![](images/71/71f89dbcee33bce284b3085b872fdb9da2cc41166fe8a0bd26ef0bb5fe6876aa.svg) 
such that 
![](images/9e/9edc744372650e86c27f31ef15ac575cc8203803bdc5fe5730390727fd37146a.svg)
Solving this system, we get the following nonzero normalized solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $\Sigma,$ and $V\mathbin{:}$

:tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find an SVD for the $2\times 4$ matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/32/325fa7080fdd5f7fc5723a2304aac049a938dfd1b490f09a7a2ceabb0b934db8.svg)

Directly applying the standard approach to $A$ could be problematic because it requires finding the eigenvalues of the $4\times 4$ matrix $A^T \! A.$ 

In such cases, it's usually more convenient to find an SVD of the transposed matrix $A^T$ and then take the transpose of the resulting SVD. In this case, we would only have to find the eigenvalues of a $2 \times 2$ matrix.

For example, if

$$
A^T = U \Sigma V^T
$$

is an SVD for $A^T,$ then

$$
A= \left(A^T\right)^T= \left(U \Sigma V^T\right)^T=V\Sigma^T U^T
$$

is an SVD for $A.$  

Going through our usual process, we find that an SVD for $A^T$ is

![](images/78/7802bcf50374a71efc4c0a7754c5628e88e7f1dfac345bc9e590cfcebd89d8d1.svg)

Taking the transpose of the above equation. we find that an SVD for $A$ is

![](images/77/77f464a1ce372dcd4e9aecb99b23342dee26fd5cf3f701ffa2fc858ebb4865b5.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "71ba93f6-01a1-54c4-bda4-b51b9b8dad77" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5110 :tutorial/title "The Singular Value Decomposition of a Transposed Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "e87c19a4-7e24-5962-880c-39d60fa71758" :step/math-academy-id 648304} {:db/id 17592186162951 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162045 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161839 :question/id #uuid "1b9d8b05-cdb6-555b-b68c-b46000bb6650" :question/math-academy-id "e-8798"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "566bda0f-f62d-581d-936d-baa8ae474e50" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050578}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162726} {:db/id 17592186162727} {:db/id 17592186370740} {:db/id 17592186370793} {:db/id 17592186423858} {:db/id 17592186423861} {:db/id 17592186430359}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the First Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix: Cases Requiring Orthogonalization"} :step/id #uuid "7cf890cb-057f-5300-9a99-426e3fb959db" :step/math-academy-id 648301 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162948}} {:db/id 17592186385970 :step/content {:db/id 17592186385971 :tutorial/content "In some singular value decomposition problems, we do not get all of the needed vectors from the usual formulas right away.

This happens, for example, when:

- an eigenvalue is repeated, or

- a singular value is zero, so the corresponding vector is not determined uniquely.

In these cases, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Solve the system that defines the eigenspace (or orthogonal complement).  

For example, we solve an equation of the form

$$
(A^T A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0},
$$

or, when finding missing columns of $U,$ we solve orthogonality conditions such as

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0, \qquad \mathbf{u}_2 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0.
$$

- **Step 2.** Write the general solution using free variables.  

This shows that there are infinitely many solutions. For example, the solution might look like

$$
\mathbf{v} = x\,\mathbf{b}_1 + y\,\mathbf{b}_2,
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are free variables.

- **Step 3.** Choose convenient vectors from the solution space.  

We usually choose simple values for the free variables to get easy vectors. These vectors should be linearly independent and, if possible, already orthogonal.

- **Step 4.** Orthogonalize the chosen vectors if necessary.  

If the vectors are not mutually orthogonal, we apply the Gram–Schmidt process.

- **Step 5.** Normalize the vectors.  

After that, we divide each vector by its norm to obtain unit vectors.

These unit vectors form an orthonormal basis for the solution space, and they can be used as the needed columns of $V$ or $U.$

**Note:** In these situations, there is usually *more than one correct answer*. Different choices of free variables can produce different orthonormal bases, so the resulting SVD is not necessarily unique. What matters is that the chosen vectors:

- belong to the correct solution space,

- are mutually orthogonal, and

- have norm $1.$

Let's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "5e93068a-566a-5c34-a459-3250d8a847d3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15621 :tutorial/title "Choosing Eigenvectors When Eigenvalues Repeat or Are Missing"} :step/id #uuid "7dc02cbe-4a5d-5f2d-8ad3-baa5e8278916" :step/math-academy-id 648305 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162946}}] :activity/title "Singular Value Decomposition of Larger Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162227} {:db/id 17592186162858 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163233 :tutorial/content "We can compute a singular value decomposition (SVD) of any matrix! The algorithm for computing an SVD of a rectangular $m\times n$ matrix $(m\neq n)$ is similar to the algorithm for square matrices.

As an example, let's consider the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/f6/f65e0eee905da85ce0be4bbf39546c2b31c2bac082ff00a6a1d54fd5b89a4a4e.svg)

Notice that $A$ is a ${\color{blue}{3}}\times {\color{red}{2}}$ matrix. So, to compute the SVD of $A,$ we must write

$$
A=U \Sigma V^T,
$$

where

- $\Sigma$ is a ${\color{blue}{3}}\times {\color{red}{2}}$ matrix with the singular values of $A$ (ordered from largest to smallest) on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal ${\color{blue}{3}} \times {\color{blue}{3}}$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal ${\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{red}{2}}$ matrix.

We proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.**  Find the singular values of $A.$ Computing the eigenvalues of $A^TA,$ we get

$$
\lambda_1 = 4, \qquad \lambda_2 = 2.
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are 

$$
\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1} =  2,  \qquad \sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2} =  \sqrt{2}.
$$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$). Seeking non-zero solutions of $(A^T \! A - \lambda_1 I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ and $(A^T \! A - \lambda_2 I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvectors 
![](images/07/07085f021218ff17060b3c1a9099e1cabad24b3d12269f97f1fe50d49b970f6b.svg)

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A.$ Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the first two columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\mathbf u_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute $\mathbf u_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $U$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix. However, we do not have the third singular value, so we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 
![](images/71/71f89dbcee33bce284b3085b872fdb9da2cc41166fe8a0bd26ef0bb5fe6876aa.svg) 
such that 
![](images/9e/9edc744372650e86c27f31ef15ac575cc8203803bdc5fe5730390727fd37146a.svg)
Solving this system, we get the following nonzero normalized solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $\Sigma,$ and $V\mathbin{:}$

![](images/c2/c2bbd771d886da6b3a369b7e03345d1be75c18c26c66590598581d2d99590524.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "670f2f0c-5dc5-54ae-9a39-2166ee2414fd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4893 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0ede58be-b8d2-5bb7-a17c-e74da723f67c" :step/math-academy-id 648291 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162945}} {:db/id 17592186163233 :tutorial/content "We can compute a singular value decomposition (SVD) of any matrix! ![](images/77/77f464a1ce372dcd4e9aecb99b23342dee26fd5cf3f701ffa2fc858ebb4865b5.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "71ba93f6-01a1-54c4-bda4-b51b9b8dad77" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5110 :tutorial/title "The Singular Value Decomposition of a Transposed Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "e87c19a4-7e24-5962-880c-39d60fa71758" :step/math-academy-id 648304} {:db/id 17592186163258 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find an SVD for the $2\times 4$ matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/32/325fa7080fdd5f7fc5723a2304aac049a938dfd1b490f09a7a2ceabb0b934db8.svg)

Directly applying the standard approach to $A$ could be problematic because it requires finding the eigenvalues of the $4\times 4$ matrix $A^T \! A.$ 

In such cases, it's usually more convenient to find an SVD of the transposed matrix $A^T$ and then take the transpose of the resulting SVD. In this case, we would only have to find the eigenvalues of a $2 \times 2$ matrix.

For example, if

$$
A^T = U \Sigma V^T
$$

is an SVD for $A^T,$ then

$$
A= \left(A^T\right)^T= \left(U \Sigma V^T\right)^T=V\Sigma^T U^T
$$

is an SVD for $A.$  

Going through our usual process, we find that an SVD for $A^T$ is

![](images/78/7802bcf50374a71efc4c0a7754c5628e88e7f1dfac345bc9e590cfcebd89d8d1.svg)

Taking the transpose of the above equation. we find that an SVD for $A$ is

![](images/77/77f464a1ce372dcd4e9aecb99b23342dee26fd5cf3f701ffa2fc858ebb4865b5.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "71ba93f6-01a1-54c4-bda4-b51b9b8dad77" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5110 :tutorial/title "The Singular Value Decomposition of a Transposed Matrix"} {:db/id 17592186385971 :tutorial/content "In some singular value decomposition problems, we do not get all of the needed vectors from the usual formulas right away.

This happens, for example, when:

- an eigenvalue is repeated, or

- a singular value is zero, so the corresponding vector is not determined uniquely.

In these cases, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Solve the system that defines the eigenspace (or orthogonal complement).  

For example, we solve an equation of the form

$$
(A^T A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0},
$$

or, when finding missing columns of $U,$ we solve orthogonality conditions such as

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0, \qquad \mathbf{u}_2 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0.
$$

- **Step 2.** Write the general solution using free variables.  

This shows that there are infinitely many solutions. For example, the solution might look like

$$
\mathbf{v} = x\,\mathbf{b}_1 + y\,\mathbf{b}_2,
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are free variables.

- **Step 3.** Choose convenient vectors from the solution space.  

We usually choose simple values for the free variables to get easy vectors. These vectors should be linearly independent and, if possible, already orthogonal.

- **Step 4.** Orthogonalize the chosen vectors if necessary.  

If the vectors are not mutually orthogonal, we apply the Gram–Schmidt process.

- **Step 5.** Normalize the vectors.  

After that, we divide each vector by its norm to obtain unit vectors.

These unit vectors form an orthonormal basis for the solution space, and they can be used as the needed columns of $V$ or $U.$

**Note:** In these situations, there is usually *more than one correct answer*. Different choices of free variables can produce different orthonormal bases, so the resulting SVD is not necessarily unique. What matters is that the chosen vectors:

- belong to the correct solution space,

- are mutually orthogonal, and

- have norm $1.$

Let's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "5e93068a-566a-5c34-a459-3250d8a847d3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15621 :tutorial/title "Choosing Eigenvectors When Eigenvalues Repeat or Are Missing"} - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e2882521-8d21-5a7b-8813-60683b9344e3"} {:db/id 17592186408023 :step/content {:db/id 17592186408020 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4a847e10-ad2a-5e19-bffe-4f473d1f4614" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407950} {:answer/id #uuid "53b3d1ac-5ba6-5b42-802f-34c001d2a3eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407952} {:answer/id #uuid "7ba9bbe0-a4bd-5d08-aca1-3c1661cf6c5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407966} {:answer/id #uuid "e36cd36f-f51a-505a-8f73-b691e55977cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407993} {:answer/id #uuid "e71af25d-d057-558a-8db8-29ad46847b17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407996}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407996} :answer-field/id #uuid "1e3568eb-62d3-583e-93bd-bbecf0a0149d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186408002}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "256724b0-7532-517f-89d9-acc3daa6cf56" :question/math-academy-id "q-98766" :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0 \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}-\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{5} \\ 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e6c10cae-3311-5de0-80be-f4f348e2b025" :step/next {:db/id 17592186408022}}] :activity/title "Singular Value Decomposition of Larger Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186407928} {:db/id 17592186408023 :step/content {:db/id 17592186408020 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4a847e10-ad2a-5e19-bffe-4f473d1f4614" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407950} {:answer/id #uuid "53b3d1ac-5ba6-5b42-802f-34c001d2a3eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407952} {:answer/id #uuid "7ba9bbe0-a4bd-5d08-aca1-3c1661cf6c5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407966} {:answer/id #uuid "e36cd36f-f51a-505a-8f73-b691e55977cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407993} {:answer/id #uuid "e71af25d-d057-558a-8db8-29ad46847b17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407996}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407996} :answer-field/id #uuid "1e3568eb-62d3-583e-93bd-bbecf0a0149d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186408002}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "256724b0-7532-517f-89d9-acc3daa6cf56" :question/math-academy-id "q-98766" :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0 \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}-\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e4884cf0-a1fa-595d-912e-314992ac2509" :step/next {:db/id 17592186408024}} {:db/id 17592186408022 :step/content {:db/id 17592186408019 :question/answer-fields A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$  select the correct options in the computations of the matrix $U$ below.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$

Now, we compute the $1$st column of $U.$ It is given by:

|  |  | {{field-1}} |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${u}_{1}=\,\,$ |  | {{field-2}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ |  |  |

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal.

Hence, we must find vectors $u=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}]^{T}$ such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to 

$$
{{field-3}}.
$$

Choosing ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ as free variables, the general solution is given by:

|  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | {{field-5}} |  |  |
|  |  | ${x}_{3}$ |  |  |

that we can rewrite as

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the two linearly independent solutions are already mutually orthogonal, we only need to normalize them. Hence, we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{5} \\ 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "e6c10cae-3311-5de0-80be-f4f348e2b025" :step/next {:db/id 17592186408022}} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186430361} :activity/id #uuid "7a17cc21-6ccb-5439-ab56-b058df3482c5" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048143 :topic/id #uuid "82e1668e-936b-52f4-a230-dc0cb3dc1f13" :topic/math-academy-id 3133} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186430361 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162712 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "46ec70b2-790d-582b-8940-37eea292ae4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186430279} {:answer/id #uuid "4d30fcb9-4e9c-5480-91f8-be9027ba4304" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186430281} {:answer/id #uuid "5ea213a0-7cb0-59f5-98bd-30dcad60aa90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186430287} {:answer/id #uuid "84575063-53ca-5b2a-94b3-9e965df7c601" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186430299} {:answer/id #uuid "d346a1ab-d6ee-5497-ae67-93ca1862ead9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186430325}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186430325} :answer-field/id #uuid "53075006-3bde-5335-a07e-7b2f11fef0a6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186161564}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0acab5c5-194e-580b-922b-276032b93c12" :question/math-academy-id "q-97365" :question/problem "$$
